rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the authorities knew Yusuf was innocent, the proofs of his chastity made them judge temporary imprisonment expedient.
rows.anchor: ظهر لهم من المصلحة فيما رأوه أنهم يسجنونه إلى حين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir conjectures that they imprisoned him to quiet public talk that could make it seem he had solicited her.
rows.anchor: فكأنهم -والله أعلم -إنما سجنوه لما شاع الحديث إيهاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the king later summoned him, Yusuf refused release until his innocence was established and he could leave with his reputation clear.
rows.anchor: امتنع من الخروج حتى تتبين براءته مما نسب إليه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says they jailed Yusuf so her conduct would not become public and expose her while clearing his reputation.
rows.anchor: وذكر السدي: أنهم إنما سجنوه لئلا يشيع ما كان منها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies the two prisoners as the king's cupbearer and baker.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: كان أحدهما ساقي الملك، والآخر خبازه

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq names the wine official Nabwa and the baker Majlath.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق: كان اسم الذي على الشراب "نبوا"

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the king jailed them because he suspected they had conspired to poison his food and drink.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: وكان سبب حبس الملك إياهما أنه توهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf was known in prison for generosity, trustworthiness, truthful speech, worship, dream interpretation, kindness to prisoners, visiting the sick, and meeting their needs.
rows.anchor: يوسف، عليه السلام، قد اشتهر في السجن بالجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two men loved Yusuf; he replied that affection had previously brought him harm through his aunt, father, and the Aziz's wife.
rows.anchor: إنه ما أحبني أحد إلا دخل علي من محبته ضرر

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud recited the cupbearer's dream as squeezing grapes rather than wine; Ibn Abi Hatim transmits this reading from him.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود: أنه قرأها: "أعصر عنبا"

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak explains wine here as grapes and says Omanis call grapes wine.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك في قوله: {إني أراني أعصر خمرا}

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima gives the cupbearer's dream as planting a grapevine, squeezing its clusters, and serving the king; Yusuf said he would leave prison after three days and serve him wine.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: رأيت (3) فيما يرى النائم أني غرست حبلة من عنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority view is that both prisoners truly dreamed and requested Yusuf's interpretation.
rows.anchor: والمشهور عند الأكثرين ما ذكرناه، وأنهما رأيا مناما وطلبا تعبيره

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: A report cited by Ibn Jarir says the prisoners had no dreams and only pretended in order to test Yusuf.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله قال: ما رأى صاحبا يوسف شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf leaves the cupbearer's identity unstated to spare the other prisoner, though the first will serve his master and the other will be crucified and eaten by birds.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي رأى أنه يعصر خمرا، ولكنه لم يعينه لئلا يحزن ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf says the matter is settled because a dream remains suspended until interpreted and then comes to pass.
rows.anchor: لأن الرؤيا على رجل طائر ما لم تعبر، فإذا عبرت وقعت

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that the prisoners then denied having seen anything, prompting Yusuf to say their question was settled; Mujahid and others give the same explanation.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله قال: لما قالا ما قالا وأخبرهما، قالا ما رأينا شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir generalizes that whoever invents a dream and receives an interpretation is bound by that interpretation.
rows.anchor: أن من تحلم بباطل وفسره، فإنه يلزم بتأويله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ahmad transmits from Muawiya ibn Hayda the Prophetic report that a dream is suspended until interpreted, after which it occurs.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "الرؤيا على رجل طائر ما لم تعبر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report in Abu Ya'la's Musnad, through Anas, says a dream follows the first interpreter.
rows.anchor: عن أنس مرفوعا: "الرؤيا لأول عابر"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf privately asks the surviving cupbearer to mention his case to the king, apparently so the other prisoner will not realize he is to be crucified.
rows.anchor: قال له يوسف خفية عن الآخر والله أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cupbearer forgot to speak to the king, which Ibn Kathir calls one of Satan's stratagems to keep God's prophet imprisoned.
rows.anchor: فنسي ذلك الموصى أن يذكر مولاه بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'Satan made him forget' correctly refers to the rescued cupbearer, as Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq, and others held.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الصواب أن الضمير في قوله: {فأنساه الشيطان ذكر ربه} عائد على الناجي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative, transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, and others, makes the pronoun refer to Yusuf.
rows.anchor: رواه ابن جرير، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says Yusuf's request for relief from someone other than God prolonged his imprisonment; Ibn Kathir calls it very weak because Sufyan ibn Waki and Ibrahim al-Khuzi are both weak, the latter weaker.
rows.anchor: وهذا الحديث ضعيف جدا؛ لأن سفيان بن وكيع ضعيف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Mursal versions from al-Hasan and Qatada are also unacceptable here, even if mursal reports are accepted in other contexts.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن الحسن وقتادة مرسلا عن كل منهما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada define bid' as a span from three to nine years.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد وقتادة: هو ما بين الثلاث إلى التسع

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says Ayyub endured affliction seven years, Yusuf remained in prison seven, and Nebuchadnezzar's punishment lasted seven.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه: مكث أيوب في البلاء سبعا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn Abbas that Yusuf remained twelve years, and separately says fourteen years.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك، عن ابن عباس، رضي الله عنهما:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the king's dream the means of bringing Yusuf out of prison honored; the king was troubled and gathered diviners, priests, state leaders, and officials to interpret it.
rows.anchor: هذه الرؤيا من ملك مصر مما قدر الله تعالى أنها كانت سببا لخروج يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king's experts dismissed the vision as confused dreams and said they lacked the knowledge to interpret dreams.
rows.anchor: أي: أخلاط اقتضت رؤياك هذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rescued prisoner remembered Yusuf after a lapse of time and offered to explain the dream; a variant reading takes ummah to mean forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعضهم: "بعد أمة" أي: بعد نسيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king sent the former prisoner to Yusuf, who addressed him as truthful and heard the king's dream without reproaching him for forgetting or demanding release first.
rows.anchor: من غير تعنيف لذلك الفتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven fat cows and green ears signify seven consecutive fertile, rainy years; cows signify years because they plow the fields that produce crops.
rows.anchor: لأنها تثير الأرض التي تستغل منها الثمرات والزروع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Store almost all harvest in its ears because this preserves it longer, and eat only a small amount gradually to save supplies for the seven barren years.
rows.anchor: في هذه السبع السنين الخصب فاخزنوه في سنبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven thin cows and dry ears represent seven barren years that consume what was stored during the fertile years.
rows.anchor: وهن السبع السنين المحل التي تعقب هذه السبع متواليات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming drought years will produce nothing, and whatever is sown will yield no return, so they consume what they stored.
rows.anchor: وما بذروه فلا يرجعون منه إلى شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the seven drought years, another year brings rain and flourishing crops; people press their usual products such as oil and sweet syrup.
rows.anchor: ويعصر الناس ما كانوا يعصرون على عادتهم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طلحة
rows.claim: Ali ibn Abi Talha transmits from Ibn Abbas that 'they press' means they milk animals.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس {وفيه يعصرون} يحلبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Impressed by Yusuf's interpretation, knowledge, insight, and good character, the king ordered him brought out of prison.
rows.anchor: فعرف فضل يوسف، عليه السلام، وعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf refused release until the king and his people established his innocence and cleared his honor from the accusation that had unjustly imprisoned him.
rows.anchor: براءة ساحته، ونزاهة عرضه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra's report in the two Sahih collections praises Yusuf's patience, saying the Prophet would have answered the caller if he had remained imprisoned as long.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another report from Abu Hurayra says that if the Prophet were in Yusuf's place, he would have answered quickly and not sought an excuse.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A mursal report through Ikrima marvels at Yusuf's patience and generosity: he would have insisted on release before interpreting the dream and would have hurried out when summoned, while Yusuf sought an exoneration.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "لقد عجبت من يوسف وصبره وكرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king asks all the women, meaning the Aziz's wife in particular, what happened when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they answer that God forbid, they knew no evil of him.
rows.anchor: يريد امرأة وزيره، وهو العزيز

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others explain 'now the truth is clear' as the truth having become evident, appeared, and stood out.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وغير واحد:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the woman's reading of the passage, the Aziz's wife admits she solicited Yusuf and that his claim about her is true; she says she did so to show her husband she did not betray him in fact or commit the greater sin.
rows.anchor: إنما اعترفت بهذا على نفسي، ذلك ليعلم زوجي أن لم أخنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She does not absolve herself because the soul inclines to desire and commands evil; only God's protection restrains it, while God is forgiving and merciful.
rows.anchor: ولست أبرئ نفسي، فإن النفس تتحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most well-known and contextually fitting reading makes these words the Aziz's wife's speech; al-Mawardi reports it and Ibn Taymiyya separately defended it.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول هو الأشهر والأليق والأنسب بسياق القصة ومعاني الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative assigns 'that he may know I did not betray him' and the following words to Yusuf, who sent the messenger back to prove his innocence to the king and Aziz; Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim report only this reading.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن ذلك من كلام يوسف، عليه السلام،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas's report says Yusuf spoke these words after the women answered the king, and Gabriel replied that he had not forgotten Yusuf's earlier intention; Yusuf then said he did not absolve his soul.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: لما جمع الملك النسوة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, Ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Suddi likewise assign the words to Yusuf.
rows.anchor: وهكذا قال مجاهد، وسعيد بن جبير، وعكرمة، وابن أبي الهذيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers the first, wife-speaker reading because the entire exchange is her speech before the king and Yusuf is absent until afterward.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أقوى وأظهر؛ لأن سياق الكلام كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing of his brothers' hardship and his father's grief moved Yusuf to compassion and tears; a report says he lifted his crown to reveal a mark on his forehead before identifying himself.
rows.anchor: فعند ذلك أخذته رقة ورأفة ورحمة وشفقة على أبيه وإخوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf says his brothers acted in ignorance because they failed to grasp the enormity of their deed; some early authorities say everyone who disobeys God is ignorant, citing 16:119.
rows.anchor: كما قال بعض السلف: كل من عصى الله فهو جاهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf revealed himself with God's permission, just as he had concealed his identity from them earlier by God's command; God relieved the hardship, as in the promise of ease with hardship.
rows.anchor: أن يوسف، عليه السلام، إنما تعرف إليهم بنفسه

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b read the brothers' question as 'or are you Yusuf?'.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي بن كعب: "أو أنت

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin read the question without the initial interrogative hamza: 'you are indeed Yusuf'.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن: "إنك لأنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common interrogative reading is preferred because it conveys the brothers' astonishment at recognizing Yusuf after repeated visits while he knew them and concealed himself.
rows.anchor: والقراءة المشهورة هي الأولى؛ لأن الاستفهام يدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf says God favored the brothers by reuniting them after separation; the brothers admit his superiority in character, appearance, power, rule, and—according to those who deny that they were prophets—prophethood, and confess their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: أي: بجمعه بيننا بعد التفرقة وبعد المدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf sends his shirt for Jacob's face to restore his sight, which Ibn Kathir says had been lost through excessive weeping, and tells his sons to bring all of Jacob's children.
rows.anchor: وكان قد عمي من كثرة البكاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the caravan left Egypt, Jacob told the sons remaining with him that he could smell Yusuf, fearing they would call him senile.
rows.anchor: لمن بقي عنده من بنيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a wind carried the scent of Yusuf's shirt to Jacob when the caravan departed, and Jacob detected it from eight days' distance; al-Thawri and Shu'ba transmit the report too.
rows.anchor: سمعت ابن عباس يقول: {ولما فصلت العير}

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj say Jacob and Yusuf were eighty parasangs apart and had been separated for eighty years.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وابن جريج: كان بينهما ثمانون فرسخا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata, Qatada, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain 'you would deem me foolish' as accusing Jacob of folly or infantilizing him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وعطاء، وقتادة، وسعيد بن جبير:

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Hasan also explain the phrase as saying Jacob had grown senile.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أيضا، والحسن: تهرمون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the brothers' 'old error' as Jacob's old mistake.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لفي خطئك القديم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains their words as referring to Jacob's love for Yusuf, which they said he neither forgot nor abandoned; al-Suddi and others likewise call their remark harsh and improper toward their father and God's prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: أي من حب يوسف لا تنساه ولا تسلاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here wara means what lies ahead: Hell waits for the obstinate tyrant, who remains there forever and is shown it morning and evening until Judgment Day; Ibn Abbas read 18:79 as 'a king in front of them'.
rows.anchor: و"وراء" ها هنا بمعنى "أمام"

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ikrima define sadeed as pus and blood; Qatada says it is what flows from the skin and flesh, or the contents of a disbeliever's body mixed with pus and blood.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وعكرمة: الصديد: من القيح والدم

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت يزيد بن السكن
rows.claim: In a report from Asma bint Yazid, the Prophet defines the clay of khabal as the pus—or, in another wording, the extract—of Hell's inhabitants.
rows.anchor: عن أسماء بنت يزيد بن السكن قالت:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Umama's report says the drink burns the face and scalp when brought near and cuts the drinker's bowels until they exit; it cites 47:15 and 18:29.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The drink is either boiling water at the extreme of heat or ghassaq at the extreme of cold and foulness.
rows.anchor: ليس له شراب إلا من حميم أو غساق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinner swallows the drink unwillingly and with difficulty, forced to take it even by an angel striking him with an iron mallet; 22:21 also mentions iron hooks.
rows.anchor: يشربه قهرا وقسرا، لا يضعه في فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He can scarcely swallow because of the drink's bad color, taste, smell, and unbearable heat or cold.
rows.anchor: لسوء لونه وطعمه وريحه، وحرارته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death seems to approach from every direction, meaning pain reaches the entire body; Maymun says every bone, vein, and nerve, while Ikrima and Ibrahim al-Taymi include every hair.
rows.anchor: قال ميمون بن مهران: من كل عظم

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir interprets death as coming from before, behind, both sides, above, below, and all bodily members.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جرير: {ويأتيه الموت من كل مكان}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says every kind of punishment would cause death if death were possible, but the sinner cannot die; Ibn Kathir explains this as the means of enduring the punishment forever, citing 35:36.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كلام ابن عباس، رضي الله عنه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After this suffering comes another punishment, painful, severe, and even worse; the damned alternate between eating Zaqqum, drinking boiling water, and being returned to Hell, as several other passages describe.
rows.anchor: وله من بعد هذا الحال عذاب آخر غليظ، أي: مؤلم صعب شديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse compares the deeds of disbelievers who worship others with God and deny His messengers to ash on an unstable foundation: their works collapse when they most need them.
rows.anchor: هذا مثل ضربه الله تعالى لأعمال الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Resurrection they seek reward for deeds they thought worthwhile but find nothing, just as storm winds scatter ash beyond their ability to gather it.
rows.anchor: مثل أعمال الذين كفروا يوم القيامة إذا طلبوا ثوابها من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their distant misguidance is working without a sound basis or upright direction and thereby losing the reward they desperately need.
rows.anchor: سعيهم وعملهم على غير أساس ولا استقامة حتى فقدوا ثوابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God bears patiently with His creatures despite their wrongdoing; if He punished them for their deeds, He would destroy every creature on earth along with humanity.
rows.anchor: بخلقه مع ظلمهم، وأنه لو يؤاخذهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God delays punishment until an appointed term rather than hastening it, since immediate punishment would leave no one alive.
rows.anchor: ولكن الرب، جل جلاله، يحلم ويستر

rows.speaker: أبو الأحوص
rows.claim: Abu al-Ahwas says a dung beetle nearly suffers punishment for human sins; a parallel report from Abdullah says one nearly dies in its burrow because of human wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الأحوص أنه قال:

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra rebukes a man who said injustice harms only its perpetrator, saying even a bustard may die emaciated in its nest because of a tyrant's injustice.
rows.anchor: سمع أبو هريرة رجلا وهو يقول

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abu al-Darda says nothing is delayed once its appointed term comes; righteous descendants' prayers can benefit a person in the grave and thereby increase his lifespan.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الدرداء، رضي الله عنه، قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists assign to God what they dislike for themselves—daughters and partners among His servants—even though they would not accept a partner in their own property.
rows.anchor: أي: من البنات ومن الشركاء الذين هم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They claim they will have the good outcome in this world and the next despite evil deeds; Ibn Kathir links this wishful thinking to 11:9–10, 41:50, 19:77–78, and 18:35–36.
rows.anchor: إنكار عليهم في دعواهم مع ذلك أن لهم الحسنى في الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq reports a saying found at the Kaaba's foundation: expecting good reward for evil deeds is as impossible as gathering grapes from thorns.
rows.anchor: كما ذكر ابن إسحاق: أنه وجد حجر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada interpret their claim to the good as a claim to male children.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وقتادة: {وتصف ألسنتهم الكذب

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir, whom Ibn Kathir endorses, says 'the good' means the good outcome on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جرير: {أن لهم الحسنى} أي: يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and others say the disbelievers will be forgotten and abandoned in Hell.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، وسعيد بن جبير، وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God will forget them echoes His statement that He will forget those who forgot the meeting of that Day.
rows.anchor: وهذا كقوله تعالى: {فاليوم ننساهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada also explains mufratun as hurried or sent ahead to Hell, from the word for one who goes ahead to the watering place; this fits being hurried there and then left forever.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أيضا: {مفرطون} أي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camels, cattle, and sheep are signs of the Creator's power, wisdom, gentleness, and mercy.
rows.anchor: وهي: الإبل والبقر والغنم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular pronoun in 'from its belly' can refer to the collective livestock as a singular or to the animal itself; the plural appears in 23:21, while singular reference to money appears in 74:54–55 and 27:35–36.
rows.anchor: عودا على معنى النعم، أو الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As food is digested, blood passes to the veins, milk to the udder, urine to the bladder, and dung to the outlet; each remains separate and uncontaminated.
rows.anchor: إذا نضج الغذاء في معدته تصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bodily products do not mix after separating, which leaves the milk pure and easy to drink.
rows.anchor: لا يشوب الآخر ولا يمازجه بعد انفصاله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls intoxicating date and grape drinks people made before prohibition and thus indicates their earlier legal permissibility; it equates drinks from grapes and dates, as Malik, al-Shafii, Ahmad, and most scholars hold, and the same rule applies to drinks made from grain and honey according to the Sunnah.
rows.anchor: دل على إباحته شرعا قبل تحريمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets 'intoxicant and good provision' as the forbidden and lawful products of the two fruits; a second narration states the same contrast.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس في قوله: {سكرا ورزقا حسنا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lawful products include dried dates and raisins, syrup, vinegar, and nabidh consumed before it becomes strong, as the Sunnah reports.
rows.anchor: حلال يشرب قبل أن يشتد، كما وردت السنة بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning reason alongside this sign is apt because reason is humanity's noblest faculty; God prohibited intoxicating drinks to preserve it.
rows.anchor: ناسب ذكر العقل هاهنا، فإنه أشرف ما في الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage also connects date and grape gardens and their produce to signs of God's creative power, as in 36:34–36.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا فيها جنات من نخيل وأعناب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates people from nothing and then causes them to die; some reach old age, when their bodily constitution weakens, as also described in 30:54.
rows.anchor: وأنه هو الذي أنشأهم من العدم، ثم بعد ذلك يتوفاهم

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali is reported to identify the most decrepit age as seventy-five.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن علي، رضي الله عنه، في أرذل العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At this age strength, memory, and knowledge decline into senility, explaining how one may know nothing after having known.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا السن يحصل له ضعف القوى والخرف وسوء الحفظ وقلة العلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, senility, decrepit old age, grave punishment, the Dajjal, and the trials of life and death; Muslim transmits the same report.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يدعو:

rows.speaker: زهير بن أبي سلمى
rows.claim: Zuhayr's Muallaqa says a person tires of life after eighty years and that one who escapes death's random blows lives on into senility.
rows.anchor: سئمت تكاليف الحياة ومن يعش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse commands moderation, condemns stinginess, and forbids wasteful spending.
rows.anchor: آمرا بالاقتصاد في العيش ذاما للبخل ناهيا عن السرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hand tied to the neck means miserly refusal to give; this resembles the Jews' charge that God's hand is tied, though God is generous, as stated in 5:64.
rows.anchor: أي: لا تكن بخيلا منوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Extending the hand fully means spending beyond one's means or income.
rows.anchor: أي: ولا تسرف في الإنفاق فتعطي فوق طاقتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses folded pairing: stinginess leaves one blamed and shunned, as in Zuhayr's poem; overspending leaves one depleted like an exhausted animal, and hasir describes an eye tired from looking in 67:3–4.
rows.anchor: وهذا من باب اللف والنشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and others explain the verse as prohibiting both stinginess and extravagance.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة وابن جريج وابن زيد وغيرهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report in both Sahih collections compares a miser and a spender to men in iron coats: generosity loosens and lengthens the coat over the body, while stinginess makes its rings constrict.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة؛ أنه سمع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet tells Asma to give freely and warns that hoarding or counting tightly will cause God to withhold from her.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "أنفقي هكذا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A divine hadith reported by Abu Hurayra says God commands the Prophet to spend and promises to spend upon him.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إن الله قال لي:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Two angels pray each morning that a spender receive compensation and a miser suffer loss.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "ما من يوم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says charity does not diminish wealth, pardon increases honor, and humility before God brings elevation.
rows.anchor: مرفوعا: "ما نقص مال من صدقة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abdullah ibn Amr warns that greed destroyed earlier peoples by leading them to stinginess, severing kinship, and immorality.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو مرفوعا: "إياكم والشح، فإنه أهلك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Burayda's father says giving charity frees a person from the jaws of seventy devils.
rows.anchor: عن أبيه، عن أبي هريرة مرفوعا:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says one who spends economically will not become poor.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مسعوده قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone apportions provision, enriching or impoverishing people according to His wisdom and knowledge of who deserves each condition.
rows.anchor: هو الرزاق، القابض الباسط، المتصرف في خلقه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A hadith says some servants are kept sound only by poverty, since wealth would corrupt their religion, while others are kept sound only by wealth.
rows.anchor: كما جاء في الحديث: "إن من عبادي من لا يصلحه إلا الفقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For some people wealth is a means of gradual enticement, while poverty can be punishment; Ibn Kathir seeks refuge from both outcomes.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون الغنى في حق بعض الناس استدراجا، والفقر عقوبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says he knows the Quran except the meanings of hannan, awwah, and raqim.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: القرآن أعلمه إلا حنانا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ikrima, says he does not know whether raqim is a book or a building.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ما أدري ما الرقيم؟

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets raqim as a book; Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it was a stone tablet bearing the youths' story at the cave entrance, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd likewise says book, citing 83:9.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: [الرقيم]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir agrees with Ibn Jarir that raqim most likely means something written or inscribed, like the forms qatil and jarih.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار ابن جرير قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths fled to a mountain cave to protect their faith from their people and asked God for mercy to shelter them and for a wise, righteous outcome.
rows.anchor: الذين فروا بدينهم من قومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer asks God to grant mercy, conceal them from their people, and arrange a sound outcome; a transmitted supplication asks that every divine decree end well.
rows.anchor: هب لنا من عندك رحمة ترحمنا بها وتسترنا عن قومنا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Busr ibn Abi Artat says the Prophet prayed for good outcomes in every affair and protection from worldly disgrace and afterlife punishment.
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه كان يدعو:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God put the youths to sleep in the cave for many counted years.
rows.anchor: ألقينا عليهم النوم حين دخلوا إلى الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God raised them from sleep, and one later went out with their money to buy food.
rows.anchor: وخرج أحدهم بدراهم معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two parties differed over their time in the cave; amad may mean the number of years or the final limit or endpoint.
rows.anchor: {أحصى لما لبثوا أمدا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths were young, and young people are more receptive to truth than elders hardened in false religion; most early responders to God and His Messenger were young, while most Quraysh elders remained unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وأهدى للسبيل من الشيوخ، الذين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says he heard that some youths wore earrings, and God inspired their guidance and gave them piety.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: بلغني أنه كان في آذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their faith meant acknowledging God's oneness and that none is worthy of worship except Him.
rows.anchor: اعترفوا له بالوحدانية، وشهدوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bukhari and other imams cite the increase in the youths' guidance as evidence that faith grows and diminishes, alongside 47:17, 9:124, and 48:4.
rows.anchor: استدل بهذه الآية وأمثالها غير واحد من الأئمة كالبخاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some say the youths followed Jesus, Ibn Kathir thinks they likely lived before Christianity, since Jewish scholars preserved their story; Quraysh asked them about the youths, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, showing the story predated Christianity.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهم كانوا قبل ملة النصرانية بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God strengthened their hearts to endure opposing their people and leaving prosperous lives; reports describe them as sons of Roman kings and nobles under the tyrant Daqyanus, who demanded idol worship and sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وصبرناهم على مخالفة قومهم ومدينتهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing their people bow to and sacrifice for idols, the youths recognized that worship belongs only to the Creator of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الذي يصنعه قومهم من السجود لأصنامهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Aisha's report, also transmitted by Muslim from Abu Hurayra, says souls are gathered troops: those that recognize each other unite and those that do not differ.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "الأرواح جنود مجندة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths disclosed their belief one by one and found that all shared it; they united in worship, were discovered and denounced, then told the king the truth and called him to God.
rows.anchor: فصاروا يدا واحدة وإخوان صدق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording 'we will never invoke' expresses permanent negation; invoking another god would be a falsehood, lie, and slander.
rows.anchor: أي: لا يقع منا هذا أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths challenge their people to produce a clear, sound proof for their gods and call those who falsely attribute partners to God the most unjust.
rows.anchor: هلا أقاموا على صحة ما ذهبوا إليه دليلا واضحا صحيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king rejected their call, threatened them, stripped their ceremonial clothes, and gave them time to reconsider; this respite allowed them to flee persecution.
rows.anchor: وتهددهم وتوعدهم، وأمر بنزع لباسهم عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When persecution threatens faith, fleeing people is prescribed; a hadith describes a person's best property as sheep taken into the mountains to escape trials, but seclusion otherwise is not prescribed because it abandons communal prayers.
rows.anchor: كما جاء في الحديث: "يوشك أن يكون خير مال أحدكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They left both the people and their religion, took refuge in the cave, and asked God to spread mercy over them and provide a comfortable arrangement.
rows.anchor: ففارقوهم أيضا بأبدانكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king could not find the fugitives; Ibn Kathir compares their concealment to Muhammad and Abu Bakr in the cave of Thawr, quoting the Prophet's reassurance and 9:40, while judging that story greater than the youths' cave.
rows.anchor: حين لجأ إلى غار ثور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the townspeople found the cave and sealed its entrance to kill the youths; Ibn Kathir doubts it because the next verse says sunlight reaches them morning and evening.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا نظر، والله أعلم؛

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave entrance faced north: sunrise falls away to the right as the shadow recedes, then sunlight passes them to the left at sunset; Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada gloss tazawwar as inclining.
rows.anchor: فدل على صحة ما قلناه، وهذا بين لمن تأمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun's path rules out an eastern entrance, which would receive no sunset rays; a southern entrance, which would receive neither sunrise nor sunset rays; and a western entrance, which would get no light until after noon.
rows.anchor: لو كان باب الغار من ناحية الشرق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain taqriduhum as passing them by or leaving them; Malik from Zayd ibn Aslam glosses tazawwar as inclining.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة: {تقرضهم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave's location has no religious benefit; proposed sites include near Aila according to Ibn Abbas, near Nineveh according to Ibn Ishaq, and Roman or Balqa lands, but scripture and the Prophet's teaching give no reason to identify it.
rows.anchor: وقد تكلف بعض المفسرين فذكروا فيه أقوالا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The youths lay in a roomy interior space where sunlight did not touch them, since direct exposure would burn their bodies and clothes.
rows.anchor: في متسع منه داخلا بحيث لا تمسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave was a sign because God guided the youths to shelter where they remained alive and sunlight and wind could reach them to preserve their bodies.
rows.anchor: حيث أرشدهم تعالى إلى هذا الغار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone guided the youths; whoever He guides is rightly guided, while a person He misleads has no guide or protecting ally.
rows.anchor: هو الذي أرشد هؤلاء الفتية إلى الهداية من بين قومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say the sleepers' eyes remained open to air so they would decay more slowly; a poet compares this to a wolf sleeping with one eye watchful.
rows.anchor: ذكر بعض أهل العلم أنهم لما ضرب الله على آذانهم بالنوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some early authorities say God turned them from side to side twice a year; Ibn Abbas says the ground would have consumed them if they had not been turned.
rows.anchor: قال بعض السلف: يقلبون في العام مرتين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Wasid most correctly means the courtyard or threshold at the entrance, though Ibn Abbas also says door and another view says ground; the word is also used as asid, compare 104:8.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه بالفناء، وهو الباب

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the dog lay at the entrance guarding the youths, in keeping with its nature.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج (3) يحرس عليهم الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dog sat outside because angels do not enter a house with a dog, image, ritually impure person, or unbeliever, according to reports; the dog shared the youths' sleep and blessing, showing the benefit of keeping company with the righteous.
rows.anchor: لأن الملائكة لا تدخل بيتا فيه كلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dog was probably one youth's hunting dog; another view says it belonged to the king's cook, who joined their faith.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إنه كان كلب صيد لأحدهم

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Ibn Asakir from al-Hasan gives the cave dog the name Qitmir and lists other traditional names and locations, without Ibn Kathir endorsing those details.
rows.anchor: سمعت الحسن البصري، رحمه الله، يقول:

rows.speaker: شعيب الجبائي
rows.claim: Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i reportedly called the dog Hamran, another claimed name.
rows.anchor: عن شعيب الجبائي أنه سماه: حمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Claims about the dog's color have no value, evidence, or need and are forbidden speculation about the unseen.
rows.anchor: على أقوال لا حاصل لها، ولا طائل تحتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God placed such awe on the sleepers that anyone who saw them would flee in terror, protecting them from approach or touch until their appointed sleep ended according to God's wisdom and mercy.
rows.anchor: ألقى عليهم المهابة بحيث لا يقع نظر أحد عليهم إلا هابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After 309 years, God raised the youths with their bodies, hair, and skin unchanged.
rows.anchor: بعد ثلاثمائة سنة وتسع سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They guessed they had slept a day or part of one because they entered early in the day and awoke late, then admitted God knew best how long it was.
rows.anchor: كان دخولهم إلى الكهف في أول نهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They turned to their more urgent need for food and drink and sent one of their number with their silver coins to the city from which they had departed.
rows.anchor: ثم عدلوا إلى الأهم في أمرهم إذ ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They had brought coins from home for their needs and spent some, leaving the remaining silver to take to their city.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنهم كانوا قد استصحبوا معهم دراهم من منازلهم لحاجتهم إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azka taaman most likely means tastiest or purest food, supported by 24:21 and 87:14 and the root sense of purifying; another view takes it as more abundant, as a poetic line suggests, but the youths sought lawful wholesome food regardless of quantity.
rows.anchor: مقصودهم إنما هو الطيب الحلال، سواء كان قليلا أو كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Let him be discreet in going, shopping, and returning; do not let anyone know about you.
rows.anchor: في خروجه وذهابه، وشرائه وإيابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the people discover them, they may stone the youths or force them back to Daqyanus's religion, torturing them until they recant or die; returning to unbelief would mean failure in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: بأنواع العذاب إلى أن يعيدوهم
